newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Bonn to make EMU grade without tax hikes - Rexrodt.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bonn to make EMU grade without tax hikes - Rexrodt.

text.p: Germany will hold to both the timetable and criteria for economic and monetary union (EMU) by cutting spending and speeding privatisation, but not by raising taxes, Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said on Tuesday.

"Tax increases to plug budget holes are out of the question," Rexrodt said according to the text of a speech he was due to give in Bonn. "By saving and further privatisations we are continuing to hold the right course for introducing the euro."

Rexrodt's Free Democrat Party (FDP) is wrangling with its senior coalition partners the Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU) over how to get Germany's finances in order to meet the Maastricht treaty target for a budget deficit of no more than three percent of gross domestic product.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel has abandoned plans to try and boost the 1997 budget by revaluing the Bundesbank's gold reserves, and has also bowed to FDP demands not to raise taxes this year.
Rexrodt said a delay to EMU could not be countenanced.
"The debate on a delay which has broken out again is extremely dangerous both politically and economically," he said.

"A postponement would be a setback for European integration. Protectionists could gain the upper hand. And the danger of a revaluation of the deutschemark, with negative consequences for German exporters and jobs is clear. We cannot allow this.
"No doubts should arise over a successful start to economic and monetary union on January 1, 1999 at this decisive stage," Rexrodt said.
However, Friedhelm Ost , a key member of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's CDU broke with the party line and said on Tuesday, that EMU should be delayed if Germany does not fulfil the convergence criteria.

Ost, chairman of parliament's powerful finance committee, said in an interview with the Neue Westfaelische Zeitung that the criteria must not be watered down and that a delay would be better if they cannot be met.
Strict adherence to the criteria must take precedence over the timetable, he said, echoing a position shared until recently by Kohl.
"The people will go crazy if we start making exceptions to the stability criteria already," Ost said.

If Germany's 1997 budget deficit is 3.1 or 3.2 percent of economic output, exceeding the EMU target of 3.0 percent, and it is still allowed to join, it will not be possible to prevent Italy from entering with a deficit of 3.6 percent, Ost said.
Kohl said on Monday both the timetable and the criteria for EMU were important, and argued against a delay, which could boost the mark and impair German exports.

Waigel also continues to maintain that Germany will meet the deficit criteria this year despite growing public scepticism amid sluggish growth, high unemployment, and the collapse of his bid to revalue Bundesbank gold reserves.
Ost said the trust of the public and international financial markets in the stability of the new currency was more important than sticking to the start date.

But another CDU parliamentarian, Armin Laschet -- who in April published an open letter questioning Bonn's insistence on a strict reading of the Maastricht treaty -- said EMU should start even if Germany's deficit exceeded the target.

"If in the fall we have 3.1 or 3.2 percent, we should carry on with currency union," Laschet told German radio. "If the project fails, hundreds of thousands of jobs will be lost. Historic undertakings should not be allowed to founder on what follows a decimal point."

Debate over a possible delay in EMU flared earlier this year when it became clear that Germany, whose participation is considered crucial to EMU's success, would have difficulty meeting the deficit and debt criteria.
But it subsided again when people realised the Maastricht Treaty made no provision for further delay of the start.
Under the treaty, the decision of what nations will be in EMU at the scheduled January 1999 start will be made next May based on 1997 budget data.
Ost said he fears that if the government insists on joining EMU against the will of the Bundesbank, this will lead to a renewed outbreak of last month's conflict.
